messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Elena Morales, a 66-year-old paramedic, had spent decades entering other people’s emergencies with practiced steadiness. The event that broke that confidence happened on a late shift when she and her partner were called to what sounded like a routine welfare check. Instead, she was overpowered by a man inside the residence, forced into a back room, and kept there for hours while he moved in and out of the house. What stayed with her was not only the captivity itself but the silence between his footsteps: long stretches in which the whole house went still and she could not tell whether he had left, whether he was standing just outside the door, or whether something worse was about to happen. She remembered straining to hear any cue that would let her prepare, only to feel terror build most sharply when there was no sound at all.

In the weeks after she was released, Elena found that the memory did not sit in the past in any orderly way. It forced itself into her mind without warning, sometimes when she was folding laundry, sometimes while restocking equipment at work. When it came back, it did not feel like a finished story she could tell from beginning to end. It felt so extreme that she would catch herself thinking it could not really have happened to her, as if she were remembering something from another person’s life. Yet the emotional force of it was immediate. If she let herself recall too much, she became so overwhelmed that she had to stop, pressing a hand to the counter or sitting down wherever she was until the surge passed.

What frightened Elena almost as much as the event was what she began to make of these reactions. She had come to believe that if a memory could break into her mind so powerfully and leave her unable to continue what she was doing, something in her mind must be giving way. She told her husband once, in a rare moment of candor, that she worried she was “going crazy.” The memory’s unreal quality only deepened that fear; because it seemed both unbelievable and inescapable, she could not trust her own experience of it. The more she took these intrusions as evidence that she was no longer in control of herself, the harder it became to approach the memory directly, and each return of it felt more overpowering.

Those intrusions sharpened her sense of current danger. A quiet house in the evening could make her body tense before she had fully registered why. Silence no longer felt neutral; it felt like the charged stillness from captivity, a sign that something dangerous might be about to happen. When the memory forced its way in, she would start scanning immediately, looking behind her in the kitchen, in the driveway, even in the hallway at the ambulance station, checking whether someone might be following her. At home she stayed on guard in a way that exhausted her and confused her family. If her husband walked in softly from another room, she startled and turned quickly, already braced.

Over time, Elena drew broader conclusions from this pattern. The fact that the memory could arrive without her consent and flood her so completely seemed to prove that bad things could happen at any time and that she would not be able to stop them. She had come to see the world as fundamentally dangerous, not in an abstract sense but in the practical spaces she moved through every day: quiet residential scenes on call, dim hallways, homes where the television was off and nobody answered right away. She was certain now that safety could vanish without warning. And if she had once believed that competence and experience could protect her, the memory undermined that belief each time it returned. It reminded her that she had been trained, seasoned, careful—and still helpless.

The job she had loved became one of the places this tightened most visibly. Entering silent homes on paramedic calls was especially difficult. She found herself hanging back a moment too long at thresholds, listening for movement, then glancing over her shoulder as if expecting someone to come up behind her. She did not describe this to coworkers in much detail, but she knew it was changing how she worked. At home, too, her husband noticed that she rarely relaxed, even in familiar rooms. She checked locks, turned quickly at small sounds, and remained watchful through stretches of quiet that others barely noticed.

By the time Elena sought help, she was less distressed by one isolated symptom than by what it all seemed to mean. Each intrusive return of the memory left her more convinced that she was losing her mind; each episode also renewed her certainty that danger was near and that she could not protect herself. She came to treatment because she could no longer dismiss this as something that would settle on its own. What she feared most was not only remembering the captivity, but living the rest of her life unable to feel safe even in silence, unable to trust either the world around her or her own mind.
